analysis.time: The study was conducted over a two-year period, with assessments made six months and two years after infection. The publication date is August 30, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The study involved 3,419 patients hospitalized with COVID-19 during the Omicron-dominant period in China, with assessments conducted across nine hospitals. The study also noted differences in brain fog symptoms among patients in the U.S., India, and Nigeria.
analysis.event: A two-year study tracked cognitive changes in patients hospitalized with COVID-19 during the Omicron-dominant period, finding that most patients recovered, while some experienced persistent or progressive cognitive decline. The study was published in the journal Neuroprotection.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Among the 3,419 patients, 67.1% maintained stable cognitive function, 22.0% experienced reversible decline, 10.8% had irreversible decline (7.2% non-progressive and 3.6% progressive). Age 60 years or older was linked to more than fourfold higher odds of progressive decline, while severe illness, hypertension, longer hospitalization, and white matter lesions were also associated with progressive decline. Higher education and more vaccination doses were protective factors.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study provides insights into cognitive recovery and decline post-Omicron infection, suggesting targeted monitoring and rehabilitation for high-risk patients. The findings are based on assessments using the Telephone Interview of Cognitive Status-40 and the Informant Questionnaire on Cognitive Decline in the Elderly. The study is ongoing, with future research needed to clarify cognitive trajectories beyond 2 years.

analysis.brief_en: A study published in the journal Neuroprotection investigated cognitive changes in 3,419 patients hospitalized with COVID-19 during the Omicron-dominant period in China, between December 2022 and March 2023. Researchers assessed cognitive function six months and two years post-infection, finding that 67.1% of participants maintained stable cognitive function, while 22.0% experienced reversible decline and 10.8% had irreversible decline. Age 60 years or older was linked to a more than fourfold higher risk of progressive decline, as were severe illness, hypertension, longer hospitalization, and white matter lesions. Higher education and more vaccination doses were protective factors. These findings could help clinicians identify high-risk patients and guide targeted monitoring and rehabilitation strategies. Future studies with longer follow-up and in-person assessments are recommended to further understand cognitive recovery and progression.
